assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new tool that opens a door: optical readout and coherent control of a single electron spin in a room-temperature solid, from single-centre detection in the late 1990s to coherent control and nuclear-spin registers in the mid-2000s. It underlies nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and biological sensing, and spin qubits for networks. This is a discovery and an invention that can be seen and verified, which fits the mandate.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group made the first optical detection of single NV centres (1997) and Jelezko's work with Wrachtrup showed coherent control (2004). Lukin is credited in the list mainly for sensing and quantum-network extensions that came later and were built on the original experiments. I would not give the prize to the later, more elegant work. I propose the original two. Other early contributors (for example Gruber and co-authors, the Harvard and Delft groups) may deserve discussion.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced by many groups worldwide for more than two decades, with commercial instruments and routine use in physics, materials science and biology. The interpretation is stable and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Exact priority and division of credit between the early single-centre detection and the later coherent-control work is from my memory and should be checked against the historical record.
Whether the committee would prefer to include a sensing or quantum-network figure such as Lukin, or limit the prize to the original optical-detection experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2018 observation of correlated insulator and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a whole field of moire quantum materials, with tunable correlated and topological phases in a single clean sample. The original experiment is clear and the scientific impact is large and still growing.
assessment.attribution: Jarillo-Herrero's group made the original experimental discovery, and MacDonald (with Bistritzer) predicted the flat bands at the magic angle in 2011. Bistritzer was a postdoc on the key theory paper; a three-person prize would be possible, but I would first test whether the experiment-plus-prediction pair is the cleaner configuration. Other groups (Dean, Young and others) contributed to the early experimental ecosystem.
assessment.maturity: The superconductivity and correlated insulators were reproduced by several groups within a year or two and many follow-up observations exist. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity remains debated, but the discovery itself is secure. The field is young, so the question is about timing rather than doubt.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is still unsettled, and a committee might want the pairing mechanism better understood before awarding.
Allocation between Bistritzer and MacDonald, and whether the experiment-only credit is preferred.
Sample-to-sample variability and twist-angle disorder complicate the picture.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a genuine invention: a unipolar semiconductor laser whose wavelength is set by layer thickness rather than by the bandgap, opened to the mid-infrared and terahertz. Its use in gas sensing, spectroscopy and security is substantial and well documented. It is an original device, demonstrated in 1994 and then taken to continuous-wave room-temperature operation.
assessment.attribution: The first demonstration was at Bell Labs (Faist, Capasso and colleagues, with Cho's MBE growth essential). The proposal of intersubband lasing by Kazarinov and Suris (1971) predates the demonstration, and the Soviet origin is a known attribution complication. Faist and Capasso as the principal inventors, with Cho for the MBE material, would be a fair three-person configuration, although the Kazarinov-Suris claim must be weighed.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of development; commercial devices are widespread and the physics is thoroughly confirmed. Recognition would be timely or even overdue by the usual measure.
uncertainties: Treatment of the 1971 Kazarinov-Suris theoretical proposal (and the fact that Kazarinov and Suris are not credited here).
Whether the MBE role of Cho is considered decisive or supporting.
Others at Bell Labs on the 1994 team are not on the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of quantized conductance in ballistic point contacts in 1988 is a clear, original experiment that showed that electrical conduction in a mesoscopic constriction is quantized in units of 2e^2/h. It is simple, beautiful in its transparency and opened mesoscopic quantum transport and later quantum-dot and nanoelectronic device physics.
assessment.attribution: Two groups reported it independently and almost simultaneously: the Delft-Philips collaboration (van Wees, van Houten, Beenakker and others) and the Cambridge group (Wharam, Pepper and others). The list credits van Wees, van Houten and Pepper. Credit is complicated because several co-authors (for example Wharam, Beenakker and Thornton) contributed on both sides, and the committee would need to settle the fair three. This is the main obstacle.
assessment.maturity: Nearly four decades of confirmation and extensive subsequent use. The result is mature and stable. The long delay may reflect the attribution problem and the sense that it is foundational rather than applied.
uncertainties: Sharing of credit between two independent groups and the several co-authors not named on this list.
Whether the impact on humanity or understanding of nature is judged sufficient against more recent candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of the skyrmion lattice in MnSi (neutron scattering, 2009) and real-space imaging by Lorentz transmission electron microscopy in FeCoSi (2010) opened topological magnetism and the emergent electromagnetism of spin textures. As a microscopist I value that a microscopy method gave direct visual proof.
assessment.attribution: The original observation of the skyrmion lattice was by Pfleiderer's group (with Muhlbauer, Boni and others) and the real-space imaging by Tokura's group (Yu and others). The theory of Bogdanov and others predates both, and the committee must decide whether that gets credit. Two named laureates is possible, but a third (theory or real-space imaging lead) may be needed.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and in many materials, including room-temperature skyrmions. The technological promise (racetrack memory) is not yet realised, so the impact on humanity remains prospective, which argues for patience.
uncertainties: The role of the theoretical prediction by Bogdanov and colleagues, who are not credited in this list.
Individual credit between the neutron-scattering discovery and the real-space imaging.
Practical impact is still largely hypothetical.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Metal-halide perovskite solar cells rose from 3.8 percent efficiency in 2009 to above 25 percent, and the semiconductor physics of these materials (long carrier lifetimes, defect tolerance) is of great interest. The potential benefit for humanity through low-cost photovoltaics is evident. Materials characterisation, including electron microscopy, is also challenged by beam sensitivity.
assessment.attribution: Miyasaka reported the first perovskite-sensitised solar cell (2009); Park and colleagues made the first solid-state cell (2012), and Snaith's group showed the mesosuperstructured cell and thin-film architecture (2012). The list supports a three-person configuration, but allocation is uncertain because several other groups (Gratzel, Seok and others) made major contributions.
assessment.maturity: Efficiency is confirmed by many independent labs, but operational stability, lead toxicity and commercial viability are still unsettled. The impact on humanity is not yet demonstrated at scale, so a prize may be premature. There is also a question whether this is physics or chemistry.
uncertainties: Long-term stability and commercial deployment remain unproven.
Whether this subject falls better within chemistry or physics.
Credit among the early device papers and other leading groups is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics demonstrated strong coupling between a superconducting artificial atom and a single microwave photon in 2004, creating the architecture used in most superconducting quantum processors. It is an important new tool and framework for quantum information.
assessment.attribution: The proposal was by Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf (2004), and the experimental demonstration by Wallraff and co-authors in Schoelkopf's group at Yale. Four names are credited; a three-person limit requires dropping one of the theorist or experimentalist contributors. I would choose the experimental lead and the two principal Yale figures, though Blais's role as theory lead is also compelling.
assessment.maturity: The architecture is confirmed everywhere and underlies multiple platforms. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so the committee must judge whether cQED is sufficiently distinct and whether recognition would be too close to that prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics for superconducting circuits.
Choice of three among four credited names, with Blais as the theory lead left out.
Applications to useful quantum computing remain unproven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, based on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties of order 10^-18, enabling tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. This is a measurement tool of the type that opens new doors, and the experimental verification is clear.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first realised the magic-wavelength lattice clock concept (2001-2003), and Ye's group brought it to the 10^-18 level of precision. The two-person configuration seems fair, although earlier optical-clock and frequency-comb work was already recognised in 2005 (Hall and Hansch) and ion-clock work in 2012 (Wineland), which constrains novelty.
assessment.maturity: Many national laboratories confirm the performance; redefinition of the second is under discussion. Maturity is high, though the broad benefit to humanity is currently modest.
uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the discovery sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Contribution of other groups (for example Lemke, Ludlow, Bloom and others) and ion clocks to the 10^-18 milestone.
Societal impact is still largely prospective.
